concepts.title: Invariants of group actions
concepts.blurb: A group $G$ acting on an affine variety $X=\operatorname{Spec} R$ induces a linear action on the coordinate ring; the invariants $R^G=\{f\in R: g\cdot f=f\ \forall g\}$ are the functions that descend to the orbit space. Classical examples: $\mathfrak{S}_n$ on $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ gives the ring of symmetric polynomials (generated by power sums or elementary symmetric functions by the fundamental theorem); cyclic $\mathbb{Z}/n$ on $k[x]$ gives $k[x^n]$; $\mathrm{SL}_2$ on binary forms gives the classical invariant theory of Cayley, Sylvester, and Hilbert. Hilbert's 1890 finiteness theorem: when $G$ is reductive, $R^G$ is a finitely generated $k$-algebra.

concepts.title: Reductive groups and the Reynolds operator
concepts.blurb: A linear algebraic group $G$ is reductive if its unipotent radical is trivial; in characteristic zero this is the same as every finite-dimensional representation being semisimple. Tori $(\mathbb{G}_m)^n$, $\mathrm{GL}_n$, $\mathrm{SL}_n$, $\mathrm{SO}_n$, $\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}$ and all semisimple groups are reductive; unipotent groups like $\mathbb{G}_a$ are not (Nagata's counterexamples to Hilbert's 14th problem live there). The Reynolds operator $R\!\colon\!V\to V^G$ — an averaging projection commuting with the action — exists for any reductive group and is the engine behind Hilbert's finiteness proof: $R$ splits the inclusion $V^G\hookrightarrow V$ as $G$-modules.

concepts.title: GIT quotients and stability
concepts.blurb: Mumford's framework lifts the affine quotient $X/\!/G=\operatorname{Spec} R^G$ to the projective setting. Linearize the action on $X\subset\mathbb{P}(V)$ via $L=\mathcal{O}_X(1)$. A point $x\in X$ is semistable if some $G$-invariant section $s\in H^0(X,L^{\otimes n})^G$ has $s(x)\neq 0$; stable if additionally the orbit $G\cdot x$ is closed in the semistable locus and the stabilizer is finite. The GIT quotient is $X/\!/_L G=\operatorname{Proj}\bigoplus_n H^0(X,L^{\otimes n})^G$. Set-theoretically, semistable points are identified if their orbit closures meet; stable points have one orbit per point in the quotient.

concepts.title: The Hilbert–Mumford numerical criterion
concepts.blurb: Stability is hard to verify directly; Mumford's 1965 criterion reduces it to a one-parameter test. For each 1-parameter subgroup (1-PS) $\lambda\colon\mathbb{G}_m\to G$, decompose $V=\bigoplus V_w$ into weight spaces and write $x=\sum x_w$; the Hilbert–Mumford weight is $\mu(x,\lambda)=\min\{w:x_w\neq 0\}$. Then $x$ is semistable iff $\mu(x,\lambda)\le 0$ for every $\lambda$, and stable iff $\mu(x,\lambda)<0$ for every nontrivial $\lambda$. Geometrically: $\lim_{t\to 0}\lambda(t)\cdot x$ exists in the GIT-positive direction precisely when $\mu\ge 0$, so instability is detected by a 1-PS that drives $x$ to zero.

concepts.title: Kempf–Ness and symplectic reduction
concepts.blurb: When $X$ is a projective Kähler manifold and $G_\mathbb{C}$ a complexified compact group $K$, the GIT picture has a symplectic twin. Pick a $K$-invariant Kähler form; the action admits a moment map $\mu\colon X\to\mathfrak{k}^*$. Kempf–Ness (1979): a point $x$ is GIT-semistable iff $\overline{G_\mathbb{C}\cdot x}$ meets $\mu^{-1}(0)$, and in that case the meet is a single $K$-orbit. The two quotients agree: $X/\!/_L G_\mathbb{C}\;\cong\;\mu^{-1}(0)/K$. This is the bridge: algebraic GIT and symplectic Marsden–Weinstein reduction produce the same moduli space, and stability is the algebraic shadow of the moment-map zero locus.

concepts.title: Variation of GIT and wall-crossing
concepts.blurb: The GIT quotient depends on the choice of linearization $L$. The cone of fractional linearizations $\mathrm{NS}^G(X)_\mathbb{Q}$ has a finite chamber decomposition: inside each chamber the semistable locus and the quotient $X/\!/_L G$ are constant, but across a wall a stable locus is replaced by a semistable boundary and the quotient changes by a small birational modification — typically a flip in the sense of the minimal model program. Thaddeus and Dolgachev–Hu (1998) made this precise: varying the linearization sweeps out a family of birational models of the moduli space, and the relevant transitions are exactly the elementary flips of MMP. VGIT is one of the cleanest natural settings where the MMP runs explicitly.

concepts.title: Moduli applications: $M_g$, quivers, $\mathrm{Bun}_G$
concepts.blurb: GIT is how Mumford constructed $M_g$ (the coarse moduli of smooth genus-$g$ curves) and $A_g$ (principally polarized abelian varieties): embed Hilbert points of pluri-canonical curves into a Grassmannian, identify GIT-stability with Deligne–Mumford stability of the curve, and take the quotient. King's theorem extends the story to representations of a quiver $Q$ with dimension vector $\mathbf{d}$ and stability character $\theta\in\mathbb{Z}^{Q_0}$: $\theta$-stability of a representation matches GIT stability for $\mathrm{GL}(\mathbf{d})$ acting on the representation space, giving moduli of quiver representations. The same machinery builds moduli of principal $G$-bundles on a curve ($\mathrm{Bun}_G$ at finite type), Higgs bundles, and Bridgeland-stable objects in $D^b(X)$. GIT is the universal stability framework.
